Photograph: Louisiana State Police US crime Former Louisiana mayor completes 90-day jail term for raping 16-year-old boy Judge admits he made mistake in sentencing Misty Roberts, who faced up to 17 years in prison after conviction Ramon Antonio Vargas Mon 7 Sep 2026 06.38 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 06.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The former Louisiana mayor Misty Roberts has completed the 90-day jail sentence she received for raping a 16-year-old boy while still in elected office and been released from custody, according to state corrections records. The 44-year-old finished her jail term on what was the Labor Day holiday in the US, one week after the judge who presided over her case rejected a request from prosecutors to force her to serve a harsher sentence. Judge Kent Savoie nonetheless acknowledged in court he was mistaken to have based Roberts’ sentence off of a list of more than 30 cases that were resolved through plea deals, unlike her prosecution, which culminated in a jury trial and guilty verdict, the Louisiana news station KPLC reported . “I asked someone to get me a list of cases similar,” Savoie was quoted as saying on 31 August. “I made an assumption, and that assumption was wrong. “I was wrong in that respect.” Roberts was facing up to 17 years in prison after jurors in early March convicted her of carnal knowledge of a juvenile – colloquially known as statutory rape – and indecent behavior with a minor. Prosecutors established that she sexually assaulted the underage victim while they drank alcohol at a pool partyat her home in July 2024. Roberts was mayor of the city of DeRidder at the time of the crime, having held the post since 2018. She resigned days before authorities arrested her in early August 2024. The victim, meanwhile, was a local high school student who was friends with Roberts’ son, a key witness in the case. After her conviction, beside her three-month jail sentence, Roberts was required to register as a sex offender, pay $5,000 in fines, submit to regular drug screenings and undergo psychotropic as well as psychological therapy after her release. She would have to serve two suspended five-year prison sentences concurrently if she violates conditions of her release, too. Roberts addressed Savoie at her sentencing on 9 June by saying, according to KPLC , “I blame myself then, I blame myself today and I will blame myself for the rest of my life. I let a lot of people down, and I am the only person responsible for that.” She also reportedly apologized to the family of her victim, saying: “I can’t give back the high school days … I can’t take away the embarrassment that so many mean people on the internet have put them through.” The victim’s mother provided an impact statement in which she called Roberts “a predator with hair extensions, high heels [and] Botox”. “Stay the hell away from my family,” the victim’s mother was reported to have told Roberts. https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: BERLIN — Germany will deploy Eurofighter jets to Latvia to help protect its airspace during next month’s parliamentary election as repeated drone incursions have raised security concerns along NATO’s eastern flank. Four German Eurofighters will be sent to the Lielvārde Air Base in central Latvia for about a week from late September into early October, Germany’s defense ministry said Wednesday. The ministry added that Latvia had requested additional support from its NATO allies to secure its airspace ahead of the Oct. 3 vote. The Latvian defense ministry did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment. Advertisement Advertisement Latvia has experienced several drone incidents this year. NATO fighters shot down a foreign drone over the east of the country in June, while another drone was destroyed in August. Authorities later said the August aircraft was Ukrainian and had likely entered Latvian airspace from Belarus after being affected by Russian electronic warfare. Latvia’s defense ministry has warned that further foreign drones could infringe on its airspace as long as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues. The German jets, from Tactical Air Wing 74 in Neuburg an der Donau, will operate under NATO’s enhanced Air Policing North mission, which forms part of the alliance’s integrated air and missile defense system. Germany will also deploy several dozen personnel. Germany separately announced that five Eurofighters and around 120 troops will deploy to Ämari in Estonia from December through March for a regular NATO air policing rotation. That will be Germany’s seventh such mission to that part of Estonia.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Jean-Luc Melenchon at a demonstration in Paris, 29 September 2026 Photograph: Apaydin Alain/ABACA/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Jean-Luc Melenchon at a demonstration in Paris, 29 September 2026 Photograph: Apaydin Alain/ABACA/Shutterstock Opinion Jean-Luc Mélenchon Jean-Luc Mélenchon will win young French voters – until they realise the size of his Russia blind spot Alexander Hurst La France Insoumise gives voice to the left-behind, and progressives approve. But many recoil from a leftwing leader whose foreign policy is stuck in 1985 Thu 1 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 05.15 EDT Share T héodore Abitbol is a self-described “militant antifascist,” with degrees in political science and comparative literature, and a bookshelf that ranges from the gender and queer theory of bell hooks to the anti-capitalist social analysis of the Marxist theorist Mike Davis. The 34-year-old is a regular participant in pro-Palestine protests, and has a decade of full-time activism under his belt: unions, strikes, protests, civil disobedience and vast protest encampments used to block construction projects, known in France as ZAD – for “zone à défendre” . Abitbol should be an in-the-bag vote for Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of La France Insoumise (LFI), a longtime fixture of hard-left French politics and a 2027 presidential candidate who is drawing significant support among voters under 35. After all, LFI is doing something necessary by focusing on some of France’s most left-behind urban areas and giving voters in them a voice: Bally Bagayoko faced down racist abuse to win the mayoral race in Paris’s inner banlieue of Saint-Dénis. David Guiraud defeated the right for the first time since 1983 in Roubaix, one of France’s poorest large cities . The party’s success in these heavily working-class and minority areas is due its willingness to draw new lines around old identity debates, and an intransigent anti-capitalist attitude. LFI parliamentarians such as Clémence Guetté are actually making innovative and radical proposals, such as recognising close friendships and extending legal rights to them. Yet Abitbol demonstrates the single biggest voter faultline between two incompatible French lefts: Mélenchon himself. I mainly remember Abitbol, an acquaintance from my immediate post-student days, as being staunchly opposed to Macron’s economic policies. That hasn’t changed. But he also can’t stomach voting for Mélenchon, he confided when I reached out to him recently, , because of the LFI leader’s stances on Russia, Ukraine and the EU. “A part of the [French] left retains a cold-war mentality where Russia is an ally against American imperialism, without seeing that Putin and Trump are in agreement about almost everything in their foreign and domestic policies,” he told me. I don’t believe Abitbol is alone. They might not admit it as openly, but I think there are millions of French voters who also crave the kind of rupture with capitalism and the status quo that Mélenchon is proposing, but have no desire to go where he would take France on foreign and European policy. French presidential elections rarely hinge on discussions of France’s place in the world. But the threat posed by Russia to Europe has already dominated the opening days of the 2027 campaign, including a special primetime TV interview with Macron . Mélenchon consistently polls at around 17%, enough to qualify for round two of the presidential election. The combined non-Mélenchon left, split between the Ecologists, Socialist party and Communist party, just trails him, with Raphaël Glucksmann leading a split field with around 10% of a first-round vote. But polling also shows that Marine Le Pen would defeat Mélenchon 69% to 31% in a second round run-off. If the divided and riven French left gets this wrong, it could leave millions of pro-European voters in an impossible position, and ultimately put Le Pen in power. The term “zombie lie” is a good way to describe much of Russia’s propaganda about Ukraine. That Nato provoked the 2022 invasion by “expanding”; that Ukraine was full of neo-Nazis; that Ukraine was developing chemical weapons in secret Nato labs; that Russia – Ukraine’s former coloniser – has legitimate claims to parts of its territory anyway. Since the mid-2010s, Mélenchon has consistently advanced many of these claims. In 2014, Mélenchon denounced the Maidan Revolution – when young Ukrainians filled the streets of Kyiv to demand a European future – saying that Russia would have to defend itself against “an adventurous putschist regime in which neo-Nazis wield a thoroughly reprehensible influence”. When Putin annexed Crimea shortly after Maidan, Mélenchon defended it by claiming that “Crimea has always been Russian”. He didn’t stop there. In 2015, in response to Putin’s aggression, France cancelled the sale of two advanced “Mistral-class” helicopter carriers – both are now part of the French Mediterranean fleet based in Toulon. Mélenchon joined Marine Le Pen in decrying the cancellation as the “vassalisation of France to Nato’s bellicose rhetoric”, and accused the then president, François Hollande, of “unbearable betrayal” for having “devalued the worth of France’s word” by refusing to deliver the warships. That is when Mélenchon lost Abitbol and others like him. “ It’s easier [for Mélenchon] to grasp at phantoms than it is to face the reality that Russia is waging a hybrid war on us, and that tomorrow it will be a ‘classic’ war,” he says. M élenchon filled the next seven years alternately invoking international law to condemn the US’s unilateral action in Syria, and dispensing with the same international law when it came to defending or minimising Russia’s unilateral action and war crimes in Syria – which killed, by moderately conservative estimates, 20,000 civilians . All while denying Russia’s former Soviet colonies their right – under international law – to freely chose their alliances by joining Nato. Accepting Georgia’s request for membership would be, he said , an “offensive and stupid provocation”. As for Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia (EU and Nato members since 2004, and some of Ukraine’s largest donors by GDP ), Mélenchon’s dismissals have been scathing . “I feel nothing in common with them, it’s the end of the world, even the Romans never made it that far!” he said in 2017. Mélenchon seems uninterested in examining why there would have been such huge interest among Russia’s immediate neighbours in joining a defensive military alliance. Apparently, in Mélenchon’s mind, it couldn’t possibly be because they had just been occupied by an aggressive and territorially expansionist petro-oligarchy – it’s because the US, and to a lesser extent western Europe, are the only ones with agency. It’s little surprise, then, that Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine did nothing to rock Mélenchon’s fixed position. Ukraine was “without a doubt” the aggressor, he claimed , whereas Russia felt “humiliated, threatened, aggressed” by the US’s decision “to annex Ukraine into Nato”. (The invasion, of course, hastened Sweden and Finland’s sovereign decisions to join.) In the four years since Putin’s war, Mélenchon’s personal blog and media appearances have been a grab-bag of the same type of ideas that Xenia Federova , former director of RT France, spewed on the rightwing news network CNews – until France issued an expulsion order and froze her assets. These included bringing Russia “back into the fold” and re-opening the Nord Stream gas pipelines; castigating Zelenskyy as “president of nothing” while promoting the Kremlin’s narrative about his lack of political legitimacy; and haranguing other Europeans for having “ demonised Putin ”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Making common cause with “the enemy of my enemy” – whatever the consequences for the less powerful – as a shortsighted form of “realist” foreign policy is certainly nothing new. (Neither, in Mélénchon’s case, does it end at Europe’s borders: “Taiwan is China,” he told French TV in May). But how is any of this principled, or leftist? After a summer when France burned and burned and burned, how is the frontrunner for the left a man who is calling for reopening the poison-drip of natural gas from a state that has been, for years, in an undeclared war hybrid war on France along with the rest of Europe? It seems Mélenchon, who has wanted to withdraw France from Nato for decades, has not updated his worldview since 1985 when he first held public office. But this is not the anti-American position it once was: it is simply to attack from the inside what Putin seeks to dismantle from the outside. Mélenchon is not trying to hide his Eurosceptic ideas any more than he has tried to hide his positions on Ukraine. What he loudly said during the first presidential debate, in late August, is also in his programme : he will “assume confrontation with European institutions” and “disobey” EU rules “whenever necessary”. This is not the way to lead and change an EU that, while imperfect, remains among France’s greatest foreign policy achievements. This is the way to destroy from within the best framework for tackling every modern challenge that transcends borders, from the climate crisis to inequality. If the new guiding philosophy is that France can decide to “ désobéir ” whenever it sees fit, so can everyone else. How do we imagine the EU maintaining its emissions trading scheme, and the carbon border tax meant to protect it? How will these – or any other European-level policies – survive if, as Mark Carney might say, a member state’s word becomes something “written in pencil” ? The short answer is: they won’t. The EU will enter an institutional death cycle, of which a deteriorating US is only slowly becoming aware. This is what Europe’s far-right nationalists want. Is it what Mélenchon supporters want? Mélenchon makes no secret of his desire for France to lead some non-aligned coalition of states geographically more remote, with even less coherent common interests than the existing 27 EU countries. What would all these other potential partners conclude if France were to show that it were ready, in a very Trumpian way, to do the very thing Mélenchon accused Hollande of doing? To walk all over its word, ratified in treaty with its closest neighbours, with whom it has shared a political community that France itself built? When it comes to foreign and EU policy, Mélenchon is barely distinguishable from Le Pen: a nationalist who believes that France is too small to do anything but close in on itself – and look to Russia for guidance. If the presidential contest comes down to Mélenchon v Le Pen in the final round then Abitbol says he would vote Mélenchon, but “with vomit in my mouth”. Pity him and the others like him who might have to choose between two equally disastrous visions of France in Europe and the world. Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. https://2paragraphs.com/2026/10/mike-pen.text: VP Mike Pence, LBJ Library photo by Jay Godwin, LBJLibraryNow , Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons President Trump announced Friday that he made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel fuel, and directed the Treasury to lift related sanctions against Russia for six months — some that have been in place since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. Some Republicans are publicly speaking out against Trump’s decision to lift the sanctions, including U.S. Representative Don Bacon (R-NE) and former Vice President Mike Pence. President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian fuel amidst Putin’s ongoing and brutal attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine makes no sense and is a betrayal of the legacy and leadership of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. While Ukraine fights for its survival, Putin’s war machine continues to prosecute his terrorist war on civilian populations and innocent Ukrainians are dying every day. Now, Instead of implementing the tough sanctions Lindsey Graham fought to his last breath to enact, President Trump has announced the United States is lifting sanctions on Russian energy, fueling the Putin’s war machine. As I saw firsthand in Ukraine last month, Putin is losing this war. Ukraine has fought the Russian military to a standstill and reinvented warfare with drones taking the fight into the heart of Russia. America should not be throwing a lifeline to Putin’s war machine. Now is the time to stand strong against Russian aggression as we did during the first Trump administration. Putin doesn’t want peace. Putin wants Ukraine. I have no doubt that if Putin overruns Ukraine, it will only be a matter of time until Russia’s military crosses a border that our troops will have to deal with him. America is the Leader of the Free World. For our National Security, for the security of our Allies in Europe including Ukraine, President Trump should rescind this deal immediately and return to the strong policies of our four years in the White House; impose harsh sanctions on any nation purchasing Russian energy and work with our allies to ensure Ukraine has the military support it needs to repel and defeat this Russian invasion once and for all. Slava Ukraini🇺🇸🇺🇦 — Mike Pence (@Mike_Pence) October 10, 2026 Pence wrote: “President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian fuel amidst Putin’s ongoing and brutal attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine makes no sense and is a betrayal of the legacy and leadership of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. While Ukraine fights for its survival, Putin’s war machine continues to prosecute his terrorist war on civilian populations and innocent Ukrainians are dying every day.” [NOTE: In July, after the death of U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham (R-SC), his sister Darline Graham (whom Trump has endorsed in the 2026 Senate race) introduced the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 . In September, Trump signed a similar House measure into law.] Pence added: “Putin doesn’t want peace. Putin wants Ukraine. I have no doubt that if Putin overruns Ukraine, it will only be a matter of time until Russia’s military crosses a border that our troops will have to deal with him.” [NOTE: The Lindsey Graham law directs Trump “to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.”] The top five importers of Russian oil are China, India, Türkiye, Slovakia, and Hungary. Some EU countries (and NATO members) including France have continuously imported Russian natural gas since February 2022. In September 2025, French President Emmanuel Macron told CBS Face the Nation that the EU’s remaining energy imports from Russia are “very marginal,” and noted that Europe has reduced its consumption of Russian oil and gas by more than 80%.
